doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

title: Gigs with Gerry Mulligan and Mose Allison, and getting the Tom Waits date
summary: After Burton he worked with Mulligan, Cohn and Sims, Getz and Hackett; Mose Allison's 'anti-time' gig; the opening for Bonnie Raitt that led to Nighthawks at the Diner.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Do you have memories of — I’ve got different categories here: Best gig ever? Worst gig ever? Most bizarre circumstance getting to a gig and getting home? That kind of thing?
Yeah but mostly I can’t remember that stuff.
Either it has to do with alcohol and drugs possibly or you know bad intentions. So I don’t know, it’s all been — I can’t think of things that were really awful but there were funny

things that happened. Like when I was playing with Gerry Mulligan in a club in New York. I worked with Gerry for a couple of years you know after Gary’s group broke up you know I played a lot with Gerry. I played with Al Cohn and Zoot Sims, with Stan Getz for a little while. You know I was playing a lot of gigs. And Bobby Hackett. You know gigs in New York mostly, sometimes on the road like Chicago or someplace. I think I went to Detroit with Stan, Chicago. Oh I was touring. A lot of work with Mose Allison. We had recorded in L.A. with Red Mitchell on bass and he really liked my playing so when I moved back east we hooked up and I did a lot of gigs with him. So I was working you know, quite a bit, and all with people that I liked. And I remember some funny things. Like after not playing with Mose for a decade and he called me to do some gigs and I went down to Philly to do a gig with him. And the first set he played of tunes we had recorded and I remembered them all so it was good, you know it really sounded good. Because you know he didn’t rehearse. So the second set I couldn’t find one. It was just — I had no idea what was going on. It was all new music. Afterwards Mose did a thing which he never used to do which is he took me, he says, “Lets go to the bar and have a beer.” You know he would usually just pay you and leave you know, he didn’t hang out really. For some reason he took pity on me saying, “I see you were having trouble there on the second set.” I said, “Yeah man, what the hell was going on?” He said, “I probably should have told you about my new concept. I call it ‘anti-time.’” I said, “Yeah you probably should have told me.” But we remained good friends and I did play with him more later but at one point in the ‘70s we played all the time, all over the place. And we did a monstrous opening for Bonnie Raitt which was really great and I got to know her and her guys in her band. And then Bonnie and her band introduced me to Tom Waits, the person and the idea, and he hired me to do his record with “Nighthawks at the Diner.” So I flew back to L.A. to do that with all my L.A. buddies, Jim Hughart on bass, Mike Melvoin on piano and Pete Christlieb on tenor. So it was like, you know, he didn’t know any of that. But his producer, Bones Howe knew me because we were friends and Bones is also a friend of Bob DeRosa and Leroy Vinnegar’s. So I followed them actually. I heard Tom Waits. I just loved what he was doing. It was wonderful. So I called Bones, I knew he was the producer. I said, “I just met Tom Waits and I don’t know, I just had this feeling — he told me he’s going to record soon and I have a feeling I’d be good for the record.” He said, “That’s funny because he just told me the same thing earlier today.”
